newsitem.title: PERU: Peru, rebels mull proposals to end hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Peru, rebels mull proposals to end hostage crisis.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels holding 72 men for more than 10 weeks took a break from negotiations on Thursday to mull each other's proposals to end the siege as the hostages endured a 79th day under the gun.
Each side had a day to analyse the other's position before Friday's scheduled tenth round of face-to-face talks aimed at finding a bloodless solution to the Lima siege.

After the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement's (MRTA) unenthusiastic reaction to Cuba's offer of asylum, attention was focused on Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's "all-inclusive" proposal for the rebels.
Fujimori's negotiator, Domingo Palermo, and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa formally exchanged their respective proposals at the latest round of talks on Wednesday.
But guarantors overseeing the negotiations at a safe house opposite the besieged Japanese ambassador's home in Lima did not reveal the contents of those proposals.

"Both sides have concluded the presentation of proposals and have responded to various questions put forward by the commission of guarantors in order to clarify some points," said Anthony Vincent, Canada's ambassador to Peru and a guarantor.
Reading from a statement, Vincent told reporters that the commission "will examine both proposals with the objective of facilitating the continuation of the discussions."

He added that Wednesday's two-hour meeting between Palermo and his assistant negotiator, Jose Antonio Payet, and MRTA chief Cerpa and his No. 2, Rolly Rojas, took place "in an atmosphere of cordiality."

The meeting was the ninth since Feb. 11, when talks aimed at setting an agenda for definitive negotiations to resolve the crisis were restarted. No time was given for the start of Friday's tenth round.
Wednesday's meeting held the prospect of the start of real bargaining after Fujimori's announcement that an all- encompassing proposal would be put to the MRTA.
The president was looking to reinject some life into the negotiations after the rebels poured cold water on plans to lure them out with an offer of asylum from Cuban leader Fidel Castro.
The MRTA is holding firm to its chief demand -- the release of some 400 jailed comrades -- and has said it wants to stay in Peru rather than accept safe passage abroad.

That defiant stance was underscored by the singing of their revolutionary anthem and shouts of "Nobody is surrendering here, damn it!" as the MRTA leaders were driven in a Red Cross sedan to the safe house for Wednesday's talks.

While the details of negotiations are secret, opposition daily La Republica cited official sources on Wednesday as saying the government's plan would include guarantees it will not seek to extradite the rebels if they fly to asylum.

Although the government would stand by its refusal to free any prisoners, the proposal does not rule out the possibility that Fujimori might eventually grant amnesties to MRTA members, the paper reported.
Fujimori has hinted at other concessions to end the siege, possibly a softening of harsh conditions for MRTA prisoners and reform of trial processes.

The rebels stormed the residence Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of cocktail party guests. They released most in the weeks after the attack but still hold their most prized bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two government ministers, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
